extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly / educated general public interested in science and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine-style biographical/obituary sketch of a prominent scientist that summarizes life, works, methods, and impact for a general but scientifically interested readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration of pathogenicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled infection experiments: e.g., three rabbits — one received an injection of pure blood-serum in the aqueous humor of the eye, two received the same serum containing bacilli (cultivated ninety-one days) — after twenty-eight days the rabbits were killed; the one with pure serum was perfectly healthy, the other two had lungs overspread with tubercles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct inoculation with appropriate controls (pure serum vs serum with bacilli), defined cultivation periods, standard observation interval (example: 28 days), and post-mortem examination to demonstrate disease causation. Include clear documentation of procedures and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermal growth limits for the tubercle-bacillus
rubrics_metrics.description: Koch determines the limits of temperature between which the tubercle-bacillus can develop and multiply: the minimum temperature he finds to be 86° Fahrenheit, and the maximum 104°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report experimentally-determined environmental limits (temperature range) with precise measurements; compare to other organisms (contrast given with bacillus anthracis) and draw practical conclusions (e.g., necessity of animal warmth for propagation in temperate zones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of bacilli in expectorated matter and persistence of infectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Koch found 'swarms of bacilli' in expectorated matter from persons with phthisis and never in expectoration from healthy persons; the expectorated matter was highly infective, and drying did not destroy its virulence — guinea-pigs infected with expectorated matter kept dry for two, four, and eight weeks were smitten as virulently as by fresh expectoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine observational microscopy (presence/absence comparisons between diseased and healthy subjects) with infectivity assays (animal inoculation) including tests of persistence (e.g., drying and timed storage). Use such results to assess transmission risks (e.g., danger of inhaling dried sputa mixed with dust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific candor and fair-minded presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific candor is a prominent quality: the investigator 'never forgets ... to look at all sides of the questions before him, and to give the fullest expression and weight, alike, to the difficulties which he himself detects, and to arguments which opponents may have advanced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present findings and arguments transparently, acknowledge limitations and difficulties, give fair consideration to opposing views, and explicitly record changes or modifications of opinion in subsequent editions or follow-up work (illustrated by Darwin's successive editions of Origin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers and methods of effective scientific investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued investigator qualities include 'powers of minute observation, the acumen in testing, and the skill in grouping data, and the boldness and originality in generalization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize detailed observation, careful experimental testing, systematic organization and grouping of data, and the ability to form and defend broad generalizations supported by accumulated facts (examples cited: Darwin's works on coral reefs and other monographs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal conduct traits valued in a scientist
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal qualities praised: 'not a controversialist ... kindly, considerate, and conciliatory in all his writings; ... modest and eminently candid and fair-minded; patient, industrious, and concentrated upon his work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate modesty, conciliatory tone, fairness, patience and concentrated labor; such traits are presented as contributing to professional respect and successful communication of ideas to both scientific peers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a compelling scientific theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin's summary of natural selection: there is heredity ('like produces like'), a law of variation (like produces slightly unlike), and high reproductive rates lead to a 'destructive struggle for existence' in which survivors best fitted to conditions prevail, so that new characters are strengthened and species arise by minute increments of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A powerful theory ties together observed laws (heredity, variation), explains mechanism (selection via struggle for existence), is illustrated by abundant examples, and offers a simple principle with broad explanatory reach (here: explaining diversity and origin of species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors influencing scientific reputation and acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation arises from a combination of pre-eminence as a naturalist (genius for investigation), methodizing observations into theory, timing (coming 'at a great crisis of thought'), building on prior advances, generosity toward co-discoverers (Wallace), and subject-matter interest (human origins) — though popular misunderstanding may accompany wide public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or attempting to build scientific influence, consider the investigator's empirical contributions, conceptual synthesis, historical timing, scholarly generosity, and public accessibility; beware that broad popular readership can produce confusion or over-attribution of credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative/pedagogical presentation technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable presentation strategy: allow the reader to form a hypothesis in explanation of the facts, only to be compelled, as the narrative proceeds, to admit that such hypotheses are 'utterly untenable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative structure to engage readers intellectually: present observable facts, invite tentative hypotheses, then show how evidence refines or refutes those hypotheses — an approach that teaches critical thinking and strengthens persuasive demonstration.
